cards.title: Structure of salary
cards.html:
Salary = Basic Salary + D.A.
+ Allowances (cash)
+ Perquisites (in kind: motor car, house, laptop / mobile, furniture, etc.)
+ Retirement benefits (gratuity, pension, provident fund)
− Deductions (1. standard deduction 2. professional tax)

Allowances are of three kinds: fully taxable (e.g. City Compensatory Allowance (CCA), Lunch Allowance), partly taxable — official allowances (e.g. uniform allowance — exempt to the extent actually spent; other allowances as per rules) and special allowances (exempt up to the specified limit/conditions; excess taxable) — and fully exempt. Allowances are governed by Rule 280.

cards.q: Classify allowances into fully taxable, partly taxable and fully exempt with examples.
cards.a:
• Fully taxable: dearness, entertainment, city compensatory, medical, lunch/tiffin, overtime, servant, warden, non-practicing, newspaper, project allowance.

  • Fully exempt: MP/MLA daily/constituency allowance; allowances of High Court/Supreme Court judges; Government employees serving outside India; allowances paid by Government to Indian citizens posted abroad.
  • No allowance exemption under section 202 (new regime) except as noted.

cards.title: House Rent Allowance — basics
cards.html:
HRA is a cash allowance (Rule 280) paid by the employer to an employee who lives in a rented house. Example: basic salary ₹50,000 + HRA ₹10,000 = ₹60,000; the HRA is meant for the rent (expense) of the house.

Exemption = lower of:

  1. Actual HRA received
  2. Rent paid − 10% of salary
  3. 50% of salary (metro city) / 40% of salary (other cities)

Taxable HRA = HRA received − exemption. E.g. HRA ₹20,000, exemption ₹10,000 → taxable ₹10,000. Under the new regime the whole ₹20,000 is taxable.

cards.title: Salary for HRA
cards.html:
Salary = Basic salary + DA (forming part of retirement benefits) + Commission on sales at a fixed %

Commission is of two kinds: fixed commission (e.g. ₹10,000) — not included; commission as a fixed % of sales/turnover — included.

cards.title: HRA — important notes
cards.html:
1. If rent paid is 10% or less of salary → HRA exemption is not allowed.
  2. Metro cities (50% of salary): Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad & Bengaluru.
  3. If the employee resides in his own house or a relative's house (no rent) → exemption not allowed.
  4. If he follows the new tax regime → HRA exemption not allowed.

When salary, HRA, rent or city changes during the year, compute the exemption separately for each period and add.

cards.title: What is a provident fund?
cards.html:
A provident fund (PF / EPF) is a retirement saving: every month the employee (EE) contributes from salary and the employer (ER) contributes an equal amount into the fund; the Government pays interest on it (≈9.5%). The accumulated amount is paid at retirement (e.g. at 60 years).

Salary 50,000 → EE contribution 3,000 → in hand 47,000
ER (XYZ Ltd) adds 3,000 → 6,000 a month into the fund
Over a career: 6,000 × 240 months + interest

EPF Act, 1952: an employer registered under the EPF Act (contributions — 10% EE, 10% ER as shown in class) runs a Recognised Provident Fund; an employer not covered by the EPF Act 1952 runs an Unrecognised Provident Fund.

cards.title: Types of provident funds
cards.html:
TypeMeaning
(i) Recognised Provident Fund (RPF)A provident fund recognised by the Principal Chief Commissioner or Chief Commissioner or Principal Commissioner or Commissioner of Income-tax for the purposes of income-tax. Governed by Part A of Schedule XI to the Income-tax Act, 2025. (Registered)
(ii) Unrecognised Provident Fund (URPF)A fund which is not recognised by the Commissioner etc. of Income-tax. (Not registered)
(iii) Statutory Provident Fund (SPF)Governed by the Provident Funds Act, 1925. Applies to employees of government, railways, semi-government institutions, local bodies, universities and all recognised educational institutions (e.g. SBI, universities, MCD).
(iv) Public Provident Fund (PPF)Operated under the Public Provident Fund Act, 1968. Membership open to every individual, ideally suited to self-employed people (not linked to salary). A salaried employee may also contribute in addition to the employer's fund. An individual may contribute on his own behalf or on behalf of a minor of whom he is the guardian.
  • For a deduction under section 123, a PPF member must contribute at least ₹500 a year; the maximum that may qualify is ₹1,50,000 as per PPF rules.
  • Contributions may be deposited in any number of instalments in multiples of ₹500, at offices of the State Bank of India or its subsidiaries, specified bank branches or any Post Office.
  • Limit = RPF + SPF employer contribution: ₹7,50,000.
